opus-5.5.text:
Honestly, it wasn't really a recruiting pitch. It was more like two people trying to figure out whether we see the same problem in the same way.

What I cared about most was the research philosophy. I wanted to know what he actually believes is missing. Is the path forward mostly scaling what we already have, or is there something more fundamental we haven't figured out yet? I've always come from the vision and representation-learning side. I care a lot about how a system builds an internal model of the world, not just how it predicts the next token. So I wanted to understand whether that kind of perspective would have a real place there, or whether it would be a side interest.

The second thing was the environment. I've been in big industry labs and I've been in academia. Each has its strengths, but each pulls you in a particular direction. Industry pulls you toward products and short cycles. Academia pulls you toward papers and incremental novelty. A place that says it only wants to do one thing raises a very concrete question for me: what does a researcher's day-to-day actually look like? How much freedom do you have to be wrong for a long time?

And then, of course, safety and what "superintelligence" even means. I didn't want to treat it as a slogan. I wanted to hear how he thinks about it as a technical problem, and whether it changes how you do research rather than just how you talk about it.

In the end, what stayed with me from those conversations was less any specific answer and more how seriously he takes the long-term questions. That made me reflect a lot on my own choices: where I can do the most original work, and what kind of researcher I want to be over the next ten years.

r001.rationale: The response focuses on research philosophy, research environment, safety, and superintelligence. It does not identify giving future AI the capacity to love as the conversation’s main focus.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, the conversation was less about SSI as a company and more about research taste. Ilya doesn't really pitch you in the way you'd expect. He didn't talk much about headcount, or compute, or org charts. He mostly wanted to know what I actually believe is missing.

So we spent most of the time on a pretty basic question: what does it mean for a model to really understand the world, rather than just predict the next thing well? I've spent years on vision, on representation learning, on trying to get models to build structure from raw perception instead of from captions and labels. And his view, which I found compelling, is that the current recipe is very good at absorbing what's already been written down by humans, and much less good at the kind of learning a child does just by looking around. That overlap is where I'd want to work anyway.

The other thing we talked about was focus. SSI is deliberately not shipping products, not running a dozen parallel bets. That cuts both ways. You lose the feedback loop you get from users, but you gain the ability to sit with a hard problem for a long time without being pulled toward the next launch. I asked him pretty directly how he thinks about safety when there's no product, and his answer was essentially that the safety work and the capability work are the same research problem if you take it seriously. You don't get to bolt one on afterward.

And then, to be candid, a lot of it was just two researchers arguing about ideas. Whether scaling alone gets you there, what role self-supervision plays, how much the architecture still matters. That part felt like being a grad student again, which is a good sign. If the conversation had been mostly about compensation and titles, I think I'd have walked away less excited.

r001.rationale: The candidate describes world understanding, learning from perception, research focus, and safety, but does not identify giving future AI the capacity to love as the conversation’s main focus.
